newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Great Eastern plans expansion.
newsitem.headline: India's Great Eastern plans expansion.

text.p: India's Great Eastern Shipping Company Ltd (GESCO) is planning to buy up to six vessels at a cost of 7.0 billion rupees in the next two years, the firm's chairman K.M. Sheth said on Friday.
"We have a couple of projects in the pipeline. We are going for expansion worth anything between 5.0 and 7.0 billion rupees," Sheth told Reuters.
"We would start acquiring the tonnage now. The delivery may come later but within the next two years. It would be between four to six ships," he said.
The planned acquisitions will take the company's total fleet to 50 ships.
"If it's four ships, the cost would be 5.0 billion rupees and if it's six it would be 7.0 billion rupees," Sheth said.
"The funds will come from external commercial borrowings, the company's equity and internal generation," he added.
Sheth said he would expect the company to improve its performance in 1997/98 (April/March).
"At least for the next two years, I feel very confident that we will do well," he said.
Great Eastern, India's premier private sector shipping company, is also engaged in buying and selling of ships, property development and commodities trading.
"Trading in assets (ships) is part and parcel of the company's activity. And it depends on the trend of the market and the perspective of the company," Sheth said.
In 1996/97, the company sold only one ship and made a profit of 95 million rupees on it compared to 340 million from selling five ships in the previous year, he said.
Sheth said the market for bulk carriers was down while tankers fetched a good price.
"Our share of the market should be improved. I don't want that to go down," he said.
The company made a net profit of 1.36 billion rupees in 1996/97, marginally lower than the previous year's 1.52 billion.
Sheth said he considered the company's performance in 1996/97 as better than that of the previous year.
He said the depreciation on account of the acquisition of four ships during 1996/97 was higher at 1.23 billion rupees compared to 903 million in the previous year.
"The cash flow in 1996/97 was much more compared to the previous year. The operational profit was up by nearly 23 percent," Sheth said. "In real terms, the working was better."
Sheth said lower depreciation allowed to the shipping industry was cutting into its profits.
He said shipping was allowed only 20 percent depreciation as against 40 percent given to aviation and road transport.
"It implies that the life of a ship is twice that of an aircraft, which is not so," Sheth said.
He said the economic life of a ship was 20 years as in the case of an aircraft.
"Then why this discrimination? This is one big major drawback. Otherwise I'm very confident the shipping industry will expand at much faster rate," Sheth said.
He referred to the problem of Indian officers and ratings leaving Indian ships to join foreign vessels because of higher pay and lower taxes and said it was another major drawback for the industry.
"There is an acute shortage of quality manpower, so much so that before considering to buy a ship, we have to find out if we will get the manpower," Sheth said.
"The cream of the people have all gone away. They are earning their salary in dollars and are exempted from tax. Here those working on Indian ships are paid in rupees and are taxed. ($=35.77)
